statement.

$$\mu_r(E)=\int_{x(E)}r_x\,d\lambda_n.$$

$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Choose a countable chart cover $(U_i,x_i)_{i\ge1}$, and replace it by the
disjoint Borel partition $A_i=U_i\setminus\bigcup_{k<i}U_k$. Choose a countable
chart cover $(V_j,y_j)_{j\ge1}$ for the target and form
$B_j=V_j\setminus\bigcup_{\ell<j}V_\ell$. These are Borel partitions of $M$.
For fixed $i,j$, the coordinate map
$T_{ji}=y_j\circ\phi\circ x_i^{-1}$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from the open
set $x_i(U_i\cap\phi^{-1}(V_j))$ onto the open set
$y_j(\phi(U_i)\cap V_j)$. The pieces
$S_{ij}=A_i\cap\phi^{-1}(B_j\cap E)$ are Borel subsets of its coordinate
domain.

By [F1] and countable additivity, $\mu_\eta(\phi^{-1}E)$ is the sum over
$i,j$ of the chart integrals of $\eta$ on $S_{ij}$. The equality
$\phi^*\eta=\eta$ says in these charts that
$\eta_{x_i}(u)=\eta_{y_j}(T_{ji}(u))|\det DT_{ji}(u)|$. Applying [F2] to the
indicator of $T_{ji}(x_i(S_{ij}))$ times the nonnegative coefficient
$\eta_{y_j}$ makes each chart integral equal the integral of $\eta$ on
$\phi(S_{ij})$. The latter sets, as $i$ varies for a fixed $j$, partition
$B_j\cap E$ because $\phi$ is bijective; summing over $i,j$ therefore gives
$\mu_\eta(E)$. All sums have nonnegative terms, so the argument also holds
when either total is infinite.

By second-order stationarity,
$\mathbb E|V(t)|^2=\sum_i C_{ii}(0)=\mathbb E|V(0)|^2$ for every $t$.
Tonelli applied to the nonnegative jointly measurable function $|V|^2$
therefore gives
$\mathbb E\int_0^T|V(s)|^2\,ds=T\mathbb E|V(0)|^2<\infty$.
Consequently the path integral of $|V|^2$ is finite almost surely; [F4] on
$[0,T]$ then makes $V$ pathwise integrable. Moreover,
$|X(T)|^2\le T\int_0^T|V(s)|^2ds$, so $X(T)\in L^2$.

The bound in step 1.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz in probability give
$\mathbb E\int_0^T|V(s)|\,ds\le T(\mathbb E|V(0)|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$.
Fubini and $\mathbb E[V(s)]=0$ therefore give $\mathbb E[X(T)]=0$.
For each $i,j$, [F4] and stationarity give
$\mathbb E|V_i(u)V_j(v)|\le\mathbb E|V(0)|^2$ on the finite square
$[0,T]^2$. Fubini therefore permits expansion of
$\mathbb E[X_i(T)X_j(T)]$ as the double integral of
$\mathbb E[V_i(u)V_j(v)]$. Splitting the square into $u\le v$ and $v\le u$,
then writing $s=|v-u|$, gives the two terms
$\int_0^T(T-s)C_{ij}(s)ds$ and
$\int_0^T(T-s)C_{ji}(s)ds$. Since the means are zero, this is the stated
covariance formula.

Divide the covariance formula by $2T$ and extend the integrand by zero
for $s>T$. Its $(i,j)$ entry is
$\frac12\mathbf1_{[0,T]}(s)(1-s/T)(C_{ij}(s)+C_{ji}(s))$. As $T\to\infty$
it converges pointwise to $\frac12(C_{ij}(s)+C_{ji}(s))$ and is bounded by
the integrable function
$\frac12(|C_{ij}(s)|+|C_{ji}(s)|)$. By [F2], each matrix entry converges to
the stated integral.

For every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$a^\top\operatorname{Cov}(X(T))a/(2T)\ge0$ because it is a scaled variance.
Entrywise convergence from step 3.1 gives
$a^\top Da=\lim_{T\to\infty}a^\top\operatorname{Cov}(X(T))a/(2T)\ge0$.
Thus $D$ is positive semidefinite. For a scalar velocity observable in
units m/s, $D$ has units m$^2$/s.

The perturbed vector field is the smooth time-dependent field
$X_H-\epsilon h(t)X_B$ by [F2]. Compactness of $M$ prevents a solution from
escaping every compact coordinate neighborhood in finite time, so the local
ODE solutions extend across $[0,T]$. The smooth-parameter theorem [F3],
applied in a finite chart cover, therefore gives the derivative
$\xi(t)=\partial_\epsilon z_\epsilon(t;z)|_{\epsilon=0}$ and its variational
equation
$\dot\xi=DX_H(\Phi_tz)\xi-h(t)X_B(\Phi_tz)$ with $\xi(0)=0$. Variation of
the transition map $Y(t,s)=D\Phi_{t-s}|_{\Phi_sz}$ gives
$\partial_sY(t,s)=-Y(t,s)DX_H(\Phi_sz)$ by differentiating the flow
composition law. Hence
$\frac{d}{ds}(Y(t,s)\xi(s))=-h(s)Y(t,s)X_B(\Phi_sz)$; integrating from
$s=0$ to $t$ and using $\xi(0)=0$ yields
$$\xi(t)=-\int_0^t h(s)\,D\Phi_{t-s}|_{\Phi_sz}\,X_B(\Phi_sz)\,ds.$$
The chain rule [F8] turns the derivative of the observable into
$$\left.\partial_\epsilon A(z_\epsilon(t;z))\right|_0 =-\int_0^t h(s)\,[X_B(A\circ\Phi_{t-s})](\Phi_sz)\,ds.$$

All integrands in step 1.1 and their parameter difference quotients are
bounded on the compact manifold and finite time slab. Thus [F7] passes the
derivative through the initial-law integral. Invariance of $\mu_\beta$ under
$\Phi_s$ from [F5]–[F6] then gives
$$\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\langle A(t)\rangle_\epsilon\right|_0 =-\int_0^t h(s)\int_M X_B(A\circ\Phi_{t-s})\,d\mu_\beta\,ds.$$

Write $\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$. For any smooth $G$, let
$\Psi_\tau$ be the flow of $X_B$. By [F4], $\Psi_\tau$ preserves $m_0$.
Consequently
$$\int_MG(\Psi_\tau z)\rho_\beta(z)\,dm_0(z) =\int_MG(y)\rho_\beta(\Psi_{-\tau}y)\,dm_0(y).$$
Differentiate at $\tau=0$; compactness bounds the derivatives, so
differentiation under the integral is justified by [F7]. This proves
$\int\rho_\beta X_BG\,dm_0=-\int G X_B\rho_\beta\,dm_0$. From [F1],
$X_BH=-X_HB$, hence
$X_B\rho_\beta=-\beta\rho_\beta X_BH
=\beta\rho_\beta X_HB$. Therefore
$$-\int_M X_BG\,d\mu_\beta =\beta\int_MG(X_HB)\,d\mu_\beta.$$

Apply step 2.2 with $G=A\circ\Phi_{t-s}$ in step 2.1. This gives
$R_{AB}(t-s)$ and proves the stated response formula.

For the correlation, differentiate under the integral on compact $M$:
$C_{BA}'(u)=\int(B-\langle B\rangle_\beta)
X_H(A\circ\Phi_u)\,d\mu_\beta$. Applying the same measure-preserving-flow
argument as step 2.2 with $X_H$ and using $X_H\rho_\beta=0$ gives
$C_{BA}'(u)=-\int(X_HB)(A\circ\Phi_u)\,d\mu_\beta$; the constant

citations.quote:
A Borel set $R\subseteq M$ is a **complete invariant domain** for this datum
if for every $t\in\mathbb R$, $\Phi_t$ is defined at every $z\in R$ and
$\Phi_t(R)=R$. The definition makes no assertion that $M$ itself is complete
or that such an $R$ has finite measure.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

Let $(M,\omega,H,\Phi,m_0)$ be a Hamiltonian phase datum and let $R\subseteq M$
be an open complete invariant domain. For any finite-valued Borel density
$\rho_0\ge0$ with $\rho_0\in L^1(m_0|_R)$ and
$\int_R\rho_0\,dm_0=1$, define
$\rho_t=\rho_0\circ\Phi_{-t}$. Then $\rho_t$ is a probability density for every
$t$, and for every bounded Borel observable $A$,
$$\int_R A\rho_t\,dm_0=\int_R(A\circ\Phi_t)\rho_0\,dm_0.$$
If $\rho_0$ is smooth, it satisfies the classical Liouville equation
$\partial_t\rho_t+X_H\rho_t=0$. For merely $L^1$ data, it satisfies the
distributional equation on $R$, meaning
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\int_R\rho_t
(\partial_t\varphi+X_H\varphi)\,dm_0\,dt=0$$
for every smooth compactly supported test function
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times R)$.

derivations.claim:
Use the Hamiltonian $H(\theta,I)=\nu I$, with $\theta$ dimensionless,
$I$ in J s, and $\nu$ in s$^{-1}$, so $H$ is in J. The convention in [F1]
gives $\dot\theta=\nu$ and $\dot I=0$. Thus
$\Phi_t(\theta,I)=(\theta+\nu t\ {\rm mod}\ 1,I)$ is complete and
reversible. On the invariant strip
$R=S^1\times[I_0,I_0+a_0]$, the reference measure has total mass one.
Take the normalized density
$\rho_0=4\,\mathbf1_{[0,1/4)\times[I_0,I_0+a_0]}$ relative to $m_0$.
Its integral is $4\cdot(1/4)\cdot(a_0/a_0)=1$.

Partition the circle into
$C_1=[0,1/2)\times[I_0,I_0+a_0]$ and
$C_2=[1/2,1)\times[I_0,I_0+a_0]$. The transported density has angular
support $[\nu t,\nu t+1/4)$ modulo one. At $t=0$ its cell probabilities
are $(1,0)$. At $t=3/(8\nu)$ its support is $[3/8,5/8)$, so each cell
receives angular length $1/8$ and the probabilities are $(1/2,1/2)$.
At $t=1/(2\nu)$ its support is $[1/2,3/4)$, so the probabilities are
$(0,1)$.

For any fixed $k>0$, the coarse Shannon entropy
$S_C(t)=-k\sum_{j=1}^2p_j(t)\log p_j(t)$, with $0\log0=0$, takes the values
$0$, $k\log2$, and $0$ at those three times. It therefore decreases between
$3/(8\nu)$ and $1/(2\nu)$, contradicting the proposed monotonicity. Here
$k$ is a mathematical scale; choosing $k=k_B$ gives the usual entropy
units J/K without changing the calculation.

The initial density satisfies
$\int_R|\rho_0\log\rho_0|\,dm_0=4\log4\cdot m_0(\operatorname{supp}\rho_0)
=\log4<\infty$. By [F2] its fine
reference-measure entropy remains constant, even though the displayed
coarse partition entropy changes.
